title: Counting Figures
summary: Count triangles, squares, rectangles or straight lines in a figure. Recognise the standard shapes first (square with diagonals = 8, with midlines too = 16; apex lines (k+1)(k+2)/2; grid rectangles C(m+1,2)C(n+1,2); squares 1² + … + n²), and count anything irregular size by size so nothing is missed or counted twice.

subtopics.title: Counting triangles
subtopics.concept: A triangle is any closed shape with exactly three straight sides, even when other lines cross it. Never count by eye. Work size by size: smallest triangles, then bigger ones made of joined pieces, then the whole figure. For a triangle with lines from its top corner, one short formula gives the count.

formulas.name: Apex lines
formulas.note: k extra lines drawn from the apex to the base.

formulas.name: Apex lines + horizontal cuts
formulas.note: h lines parallel to the base, each crossing every apex line.

tricks.title: Square with diagonals: 8 or 16
tricks.body: A rectangle with both diagonals always has 8 triangles. Add both midlines and it becomes 16. Memorise both.

example.q: How many triangles are there in a square with both diagonals and both midlines drawn?
steps: Two-piece triangles, full side as base: 4.

tricks.title: Count the lines, then choose two
tricks.body: In an apex figure, count the lines through the apex (extra lines plus both sides) and choose any two of them.

example.q: A triangle has 4 lines drawn from its apex to the base. How many triangles are there?

mistakes.right: After the smallest, hunt joined pieces of 2 and 3 parts, then the whole figure.

mistakes.wrong: Counting a four-sided pointed region as a triangle.
mistakes.right: Trace the border. Only exactly three straight pieces count.
End every count by asking: is the whole figure itself one more triangle?

mistakes.wrong: Taking k as the number of base parts.
mistakes.right: k is the number of extra apex lines. The base has k + 1 parts, not k.

mistakes.wrong: Multiplying by h instead of h + 1 for horizontal cuts.
mistakes.right: The base itself is also a base line, so the multiplier is h + 1.

mistakes.wrong: Skipping the upside-down triangles in row figures.
mistakes.right: Count upright sizes first, then hunt the upside-down ones between them.

subtopics.notes:
### What counts as a triangle
A triangle is a closed shape with exactly three straight sides. A side can pass through other lines on the way. So a big shape made of joined pieces still counts.

Think of a cut samosa. Each cut makes new pieces. Two small pieces joined together can still form one big triangle. Most wrong answers miss these bigger triangles.

> **Rule:** Count every closed shape whose border has exactly three straight pieces. Extra lines inside it do not matter.

### Count size by size
Never count everything at once. Go from smallest to biggest.

1. Count the smallest triangles. These have no line inside.
2. Count triangles made of 2 joined pieces, then 3 pieces, and so on.
3. Count the whole figure if it is itself a triangle.
4. Add the groups.

A square with both diagonals: 4 smallest triangles meet at the centre. 4 halves use a full side as base. Total $4+4=8$.

> **Tip:** Write each group's count beside the figure. Adding group totals is safer than one running count.

### Name the corners for odd figures
Some figures fit no formula: overlapping triangles, house shapes, mixed lines. Label every corner and every crossing point with a letter.

List triangles one point at a time. For each point, find triangles using only the lines actually drawn there. This is slow but nothing gets counted twice.

### The apex formula
One common figure: a triangle with $k$ extra lines from its top corner (the apex) to the base.

Every triangle here uses the apex plus two of the $k+2$ lines through it. Choosing any two of them gives:
$$T=\dfrac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}$$
With 3 apex lines: $4\times5\div2=10$ triangles.

> **Watch:** $k$ counts only the extra lines. The two sides of the big triangle are added on top, giving $k+2$.

### Horizontal cuts multiply
Now add $h$ lines parallel to the base, each crossing every apex line. Each cut is one more base line, so the whole set repeats per base:
$$T=\dfrac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}\times(h+1)$$
With 2 apex lines and 1 cut: $6\times2=12$ triangles.

> **Watch:** A cut counts only if it crosses every apex line. A short cut that stops early breaks the formula.

### Famous figures worth memorising
Exam figures repeat every year. Learn these totals; each is verified above.

| Figure | Triangles |
|---|---|
| Square (any rectangle) with both diagonals | 8 |
| Same square plus both midlines | 16 |
| Triangle with all 3 medians | 16 |
| Pentagon with all 5 diagonals (star) | 35 |

A triangle split into rows of small triangles gives 1, 5, 13, 27, 48 for 1 to 5 rows. Upside-down triangles count too: 3 rows give 10 upright and 3 upside-down, total 13.

patterns.name: Triangle with lines from the apex (and horizontal cuts)
patterns.howToSpot: One big triangle; several lines run from its top corner to the base; sometimes lines parallel to the base cross them all.
steps: Count k, the extra lines from the apex.
Count h, the lines parallel to the base that cross every apex line.
Multiply by (h + 1), one factor per base line.
patterns.why: Every triangle picks two of the k + 2 lines through the apex and one of the h + 1 base lines, so the choices multiply.

example.q: A triangle has 3 lines drawn from its apex to the base, and 1 line parallel to the base crossing all of them. How many triangles are there?

patterns.name: Square or rectangle with diagonals and midlines
patterns.howToSpot: A square or rectangle with one or both diagonals, often with the lines joining the middles of opposite sides.
steps: Count the smallest triangles around the centre.
Count two-piece triangles with a full side as base.
Count the half-squares along each diagonal.
patterns.why: The figure is symmetric, so each size comes in a set of four and one representative settles the group.

example.q: A square has both diagonals and both midlines drawn. How many triangles are there?

patterns.name: Triangle divided into rows of small triangles
patterns.howToSpot: A big triangle filled with small triangles, some pointing up and some pointing down.
steps: Count n, the number of rows (parts on each side).
Upright triangles of size s: (n − s + 1)(n − s + 2) ÷ 2, for every s.
Then count the upside-down ones, usually only the small size.
patterns.why: Upright triangles of one size sit in a triangular number of positions; the upside-down ones hide between them.

example.q: A triangle is divided into 3 rows of small triangles. How many triangles are there?

patterns.name: Triangle with lines from its corners (medians and cevians)
patterns.howToSpot: A triangle with lines from one or more corners to the opposite sides, crossing inside.
steps: Label every corner and inside crossing point.
Count the smallest triangles around each crossing.
Look for joined pieces and half-triangles along each drawn line.
patterns.why: The crossing points split each line into levels, so triangles appear at several sizes; labelling keeps them apart.

example.q: In a triangle, all three medians are drawn. How many triangles are formed?
steps: A full side as base, centre as top: 3.
Each median halves the big triangle: 6 halves.

patterns.name: Irregular composite figures (house, star, pentagon)
patterns.howToSpot: A figure built from several shapes: a house with a roof, a star inside a pentagon, two overlapping triangles.
steps: Break the figure into known parts (square with diagonals = 8, and so on).
Count triangles fully inside each part.
Count triangles that cross from one part into another.
patterns.why: Known sub-figures give quick totals; only the triangles crossing between parts need fresh work.

example.q: A regular pentagon has all 5 of its diagonals drawn, forming a star inside. How many triangles are there?
steps: Triangles using 3 outer corners: choose any 3 of 5 = 10.

revision: Count size by size: smallest, then joined pieces, then the whole figure.
Apex lines: $T=\dfrac{(k+1)(k+2)}{2}$; with h horizontal cuts multiply by $h+1$.
Square with 2 diagonals = 8; add both midlines = 16.
Row figures: 1, 5, 13, 27, 48 triangles for 1 to 5 rows.
Triangle with 3 medians = 16; pentagon with all diagonals = 35.
No formula fits? Label every corner and crossing point, then list triangles.

subtopics.title: Counting squares and rectangles
subtopics.concept: In a grid, count squares and rectangles by choosing lines, not by eye. Any 2 vertical grid lines and any 2 horizontal ones frame exactly one rectangle. For squares, go size by size: 1 by 1, then 2 by 2, and so on. Every square is also a rectangle, so rectangle counts include squares.

formulas.name: Rectangles in an m × n grid
formulas.note: Pick 2 of the m + 1 vertical lines and 2 of the n + 1 horizontal lines.

formulas.name: Squares in an m × n grid
formulas.note: An n × n grid gives 1 squared + 2 squared + ... + n squared.

tricks.title: Line-pair trick
tricks.body: A rectangle is decided by its two vertical sides and two horizontal sides. Count line pairs, never shapes.

example.q: How many rectangles are there in a 3 × 2 grid?

tricks.title: Memorise the small grids
tricks.body: 2 × 2: 5 squares, 9 rectangles. 3 × 3: 14 squares, 36 rectangles. 4 × 4: 30 squares, 100 rectangles. They appear inside bigger questions.

example.q: How many squares are there in a 4 × 4 grid?

mistakes.wrong: Leaving squares out when the question asks for rectangles.
mistakes.right: Every square is a rectangle. Subtract them only when the question says non-square.

mistakes.wrong: Using the number of cells instead of lines in the choose-2 count.
mistakes.right: A grid with m columns has m + 1 lines. Choose 2 of the lines.

mistakes.wrong: Missing the bigger squares (2 × 2, 3 × 3) in a grid.
mistakes.right: Count size by size up to the smaller side of the grid.

mistakes.wrong: Counting a tilted square's triangle pieces as more squares.
mistakes.right: Grid lines through a diamond cut it into triangles, not squares.

mistakes.wrong: Applying the grid formula to a plus or L shape.
mistakes.right: Irregular shapes need a side-by-side check: all four sides drawn, inside filled.

subtopics.notes:
### Every square is a rectangle
A rectangle has four sides and four right angles. A square is a rectangle with all four sides equal. So when a question asks for rectangles, the squares are inside the count. Only the phrase "rectangles that are not squares" leaves them out.

### Count squares size by size
In a grid of m columns and n rows, count each size separately.

- 1 × 1 squares: $m\times n$
- 2 × 2 squares: $(m-1)(n-1)$
- 3 × 3 squares: $(m-2)(n-2)$, and so on.

A 4 × 3 grid: $12+6+2=20$ squares. For a square n × n grid the total is $1^2+2^2+\dots+n^2$. A chessboard: $1+4+9+\dots+64=204$ squares.

> **Tip:** Stop when the square's side reaches the smaller of m and n. Bigger squares simply do not fit.

### Count rectangles by picking lines
Never hunt shapes. A rectangle is fixed the moment you pick its two vertical sides and its two horizontal sides.

A grid with m columns has $m+1$ vertical lines. With n rows it has $n+1$ horizontal lines. Pick any 2 of each:
$$R=\binom{m+1}{2}\times\binom{n+1}{2}=\frac{m(m+1)}{2}\times\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$$
A 3 × 2 grid: $6\times3=18$ rectangles. A single row of m cells has $\dfrac{m(m+1)}{2}$ rectangles.

### Rectangles that are not squares
Some questions ask for rectangles that are not squares. Count all rectangles, then subtract the squares: $R-S$.

A 3 × 3 grid: $36-14=22$ rectangles that are not squares.

> **Watch:** Options love to offer R and S alone. Read whether the question wants all rectangles or only the non-square ones.

### Check with a small grid
When you forget a formula, test it on a tiny grid you can count by eye.

A 2 × 2 grid has 4 small squares and 1 big square, so 5 squares. It has 9 rectangles: 4 single cells, 4 two-cell blocks and 1 whole grid. The formula gives $3\times3=9$, so it works.

### Tilted squares
Join the middles of a square's four sides and you get a tilted square, a diamond. It counts as a square too.

A square with both midlines and the diamond: 4 small squares + 1 big square + 1 diamond = 6 squares. The midlines cut the diamond into 4 triangles, so no extra squares hide inside it.

> **Watch:** A tilted square needs all four sides fully drawn. Grid lines crossing a diamond only make triangles.

### Irregular grids
Plus signs, L shapes and grids with missing lines break the formulas. Check every candidate by hand.

1. Count the single cells.
2. For each bigger square or rectangle, check that all four sides are drawn.
3. Check the inside is completely filled.

Five equal squares in a plus sign: 5 single cells + 4 two-cell blocks + 1 full row + 1 full column = 11 rectangles.

> **Example:** A missing middle line kills every rectangle that needs it as a side. Always trace the four sides.

patterns.name: Squares in a grid
patterns.howToSpot: A chessboard-like grid; the question asks for squares of all sizes.
steps: Note m columns and n rows.
Add (m − k + 1)(n − k + 1) for k = 1, 2, ... up to the smaller side.
For an n × n grid use 1 squared + 2 squared + ... + n squared.
patterns.why: A k by k square fits in (m − k + 1) places across and (n − k + 1) places down.

example.q: How many squares are there in a 4 × 4 grid?

patterns.name: Rectangles in a grid
patterns.howToSpot: A grid of cells; the question asks for rectangles (squares included).
steps: Count the vertical lines (m + 1) and horizontal lines (n + 1).
patterns.why: Choosing 2 vertical and 2 horizontal lines fixes exactly one rectangle.

example.q: How many rectangles are there in a grid of 4 columns and 3 rows?

patterns.name: Squares with a tilted (diamond) square inside
patterns.howToSpot: A square or grid with lines joining the middles of the sides, forming a diamond.
steps: Count the upright squares of the grid.
Add each tilted square whose four sides are fully drawn.
Do not count the triangles made where grid lines cut the diamond.
patterns.why: A tilted square is a square too, but grid lines through it only create triangles.

example.q: A square is divided into 4 equal squares by its two midlines, and the midpoints of its four sides are joined to form a diamond. How many squares are there?

patterns.name: Irregular grids (plus, L-shape, missing lines)
patterns.howToSpot: Cells joined in a cross or L shape, or a grid with a line missing.
steps: For each bigger shape, check all four sides are drawn.
For rectangles, fix a top-left cell and extend right and down while the region stays filled.
patterns.why: The grid formulas assume every line runs the full width; here they do not.

example.q: Five equal squares form a plus sign (one centre square, one on each side). How many rectangles are there?

patterns.name: Rectangles that are not squares
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'rectangles which are not squares'.
steps: Count all rectangles with the line-pair method.
Count the squares size by size.
patterns.why: The full count includes squares, so removing the squares leaves exactly the rest.

example.q: How many rectangles in a 3 × 3 grid are not squares?

revision: Squares in an $m\times n$ grid: add $(m-k+1)(n-k+1)$ for each size k.
Tilted squares count once; irregular grids need a four-sides check.

subtopics.title: Counting straight lines
subtopics.concept: Count each complete straight path once, however many pieces it is drawn in. Two pieces on one path, touching end to end, are one line. Sweep the figure direction by direction: horizontals, verticals, then each slant direction separately. Curves and arcs are never straight lines.

formulas.name: Lines in a grid
formulas.note: m columns, n rows; add extra slanting lines separately.

tricks.title: Direction sweep
tricks.body: One pass for horizontals, one for verticals, one per slant direction. The running total is the answer.

example.q: How many straight lines are there in a square with both diagonals drawn?

tricks.title: Merge before counting
tricks.body: When cell diagonals sit end to end on one path, they are one line. Join them in your head first.

example.q: A 2 × 2 grid has both diagonals drawn in every cell. How many straight lines are there?
steps: Down-right: the 2 pieces on the main path join, plus one line on each side = 3.

mistakes.wrong: Counting each piece of one straight path as a separate line.
mistakes.right: Pieces on one path that touch end to end are a single line.
The four sides of the frame are lines too. Sweep them first.

mistakes.wrong: Counting arcs and circles as lines.
mistakes.right: Only straight paths count. Curves are ignored in line questions.
Finish one direction completely before starting the next.

mistakes.wrong: Using (m + 1) + (n + 1) when a grid line stops halfway.
mistakes.right: The formula needs full-length lines. Count broken grids by hand.

subtopics.notes:
### One path is one line
Count each complete straight path once, even if it is drawn as many pieces. Two pieces on the same path, touching end to end, make one line. Two pieces with a gap between them make two lines.

Think of a road crossing ten junctions. It is still one road. Only a new direction, or a gap, starts a new line.

> **Rule:** Count paths, not pieces. Every crossing point cuts a line into pieces that rejoin into one line.

### The direction sweep
Count one direction at a time. This makes double counting impossible.

1. Count horizontal lines, from top to bottom.
2. Count vertical lines, from left to right.
3. Count each slant direction separately: down-to-right first, then down-to-left.
4. Add the groups.

A square with both diagonals and both midlines: 3 horizontal + 3 vertical + 2 slanting = 8 lines.

> **Tip:** Say the direction out loud as you tick lines off. Turning the page a little helps slants stand out.

### Grids
A grid of m columns and n rows has m + 1 vertical lines and n + 1 horizontal lines:
$$L=(m+1)+(n+1)$$
A 3 × 2 grid needs $4+3=7$ lines. A 5 × 4 grid needs $6+5=11$ lines.

If the long diagonals of the whole grid are also drawn, add them as extra slanting lines.

### When pieces join into one line
The classic trap: a grid where every small cell has its own diagonals. Pieces sitting on one path join into a single line.

Take a 2 × 2 grid with both diagonals drawn in all 4 cells. That is 6 grid lines plus 8 cell-diagonal pieces. On the main path, two cell diagonals touch end to end and join into one long line. The same happens on the other path. So the 8 pieces form only 6 lines: 4 short ones plus 2 long ones.

Total: $6+6=12$ lines, not $6+8=14$.

> **Watch:** Merge the pieces first, then count. Never count drawn pieces directly as lines.

### Stars and polygons
Star figures are built from long lines that cross each other.

- A five-point star (pentagram) is drawn with 5 lines.
- A six-point star made of two triangles has 6 lines.
- A hexagon with its 3 long diagonals has $6+3=9$ lines.
- A triangle cut into rows has 3 directions, each with one line per row: 3 rows give $3\times3=9$ lines.

> **Example:** Count the pentagram's strokes: each of the 5 points is made by 2 strokes, and each stroke serves 2 points. So $5\times2\div2=5$ lines.

### Curves do not count
A straight line has no bend anywhere. Circles, arcs and wavy strokes are not straight lines, so skip them. If the question asks for one direction only, count just that direction and ignore everything else.

patterns.name: Total straight lines in a square/rectangle figure
patterns.howToSpot: A square or rectangle with diagonals, midlines or cell diagonals; asks for straight lines.
steps: Count each slant direction, merging pieces that share one path.
patterns.why: Grouping by direction makes double counting impossible.

example.q: A square has both diagonals and both midlines drawn. How many straight lines are there?
steps: Horizontal: top side, midline, bottom side = 3.

patterns.name: Count lines of one direction only
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks only for horizontal, vertical or slanting lines.
steps: Scan the whole figure and tick each separate line of that direction.
Check for pieces that join on one path.
patterns.why: The other directions do not matter, so all attention goes to one sweep.

example.q: A 3 × 2 grid also has both long diagonals of the whole rectangle drawn. How many vertical lines are there?
steps: The two diagonals are slanting, not vertical.

patterns.name: Stars, polygons and triangle grids
patterns.howToSpot: A star, a hexagon with diagonals, or a triangle filled with small triangles.
steps: Find the long straight paths that build the figure.
Count paths, not the small pieces between crossings.
For row figures, count lines per direction, then multiply by 3 directions.
patterns.why: Each long line is cut into many pieces by the others; the pieces are not separate lines.

example.q: How many straight lines are needed to draw a five-point star?
steps: Each point is made by 2 strokes.
Each stroke also serves a second point.

patterns.name: Straight lines in a grid
patterns.howToSpot: A plain grid, sometimes with long diagonals drawn across it.
steps: Add any extra diagonal paths, one per full path.
patterns.why: Every grid line runs the full width or height, so each gives exactly one line.

example.q: How many straight lines are there in a grid of 5 columns and 4 rows?

patterns.name: Pieces that join on one path
patterns.howToSpot: A grid where every cell has its own diagonals, or a figure with collinear touching strokes.
steps: Draw or imagine each diagonal path across the whole figure.
Join pieces that touch end to end on it.
Count one line per merged path, per direction.
patterns.why: Touching collinear pieces are one straight path, so they are one line, not two.

example.q: A 2 × 2 grid has both diagonals drawn in every one of its 4 cells. How many straight lines are there?
steps: Down-right: 8 pieces form 3 paths (the 2 middle pieces join).

revision: One straight path = one line, however many pieces it is drawn in.
Sweep: horizontals, verticals, then each slant direction.
Grid of m columns, n rows: (m + 1) + (n + 1) lines.
Square + 2 diagonals = 6 lines; add both midlines = 8.
Pentagram 5, six-point star 6, hexagon with 3 long diagonals 9.
Join collinear pieces first; ignore curves.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A triangle with several lines from the top corner to the base, sometimes with lines parallel to the base.
pyqPatterns.approach: Count the apex lines k and the parallel cuts h. Use (k+1)(k+2)/2 × (h+1). No need to count by eye.

example.q: A triangle has 4 lines from the apex to the base. How many triangles?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A square or rectangle with diagonals and midlines, or a row of such squares.
pyqPatterns.approach: Count by size: smallest pieces, then 2-piece triangles, then half-squares. Square with diagonals = 8; with midlines too = 16.

example.q: How many triangles are in a square with both diagonals?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A big triangle made of small upright and upside-down triangles.
pyqPatterns.approach: Use 1, 5, 13, 27, 48 for 1 to 5 rows. Do not forget the upside-down triangles.

example.q: A triangle is split into 4 rows of small triangles. How many triangles?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: House shapes, pentagon with a star, two overlapping triangles, a triangle with medians.
pyqPatterns.approach: Label corners and crossings; count triangles part by part, then the ones crossing parts. Known values: medians 16, pentagon with diagonals 35.

example.q: How many triangles are formed when all three medians of a triangle are drawn?

pyqPatterns.approach: Add (m−k+1)(n−k+1) for every size k. For n × n: 1² + … + n².

example.q: How many squares are there on a 5 × 5 grid?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A grid; count all rectangles, squares included.
pyqPatterns.approach: Choose 2 vertical and 2 horizontal lines: C(m+1,2) × C(n+1,2).

example.q: How many rectangles are there in a 3 × 3 grid?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A diamond drawn inside a square or grid, or cells arranged in a plus or L shape.
pyqPatterns.approach: Count upright squares first, then add each tilted square whose four sides are drawn. For irregular grids, check all four sides of each candidate.

example.q: A 2 × 2 grid has a diamond joining the middles of its outer sides. How many squares?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: How many straight lines are there, or the least number of lines needed to draw a figure.
pyqPatterns.approach: Sweep direction by direction; pieces on one straight path count once. Pentagram = 5, grid = (m+1)+(n+1).

solvedExamples.solution: Horizontal: top and bottom of the rectangle → 2. Vertical: two sides → 2. Diagonals of the rectangle → 2. Roof slopes → 2. Total **8**.

practice.solution: Sweep one direction at a time. Horizontal: 2. Vertical: 3. Slanting: 2. Total = 2 + 3 + 2 = **7**.

practice.q: How many **slanting** straight lines are there in the given figure?
practice.solution: Slanting lines are neither horizontal nor vertical. The square has 2 diagonals and the roof has 2 sloping sides. The roof sides do not lie on the diagonals' paths, so they are separate lines. Total = **4**.

practice.q: How many **horizontal** straight lines are there in the given figure?
practice.solution: The big triangle has 4 rows of small triangles. There is one horizontal line under each row, the base included, and the top corner is only a point. Horizontal lines = **4**. (All lines together would be 12.)

practice.q: How many **slanting** straight lines are there in the given figure?
practice.solution: The square's 2 diagonals are slanting. The diamond has 4 sides; each is parallel to a diagonal but lies on a different path, so each is a separate line. Total slanting lines = 2 + 4 = **6**.
practice.shortcut: Parallel is not the same as in-line.

practice.q: What is the minimum number of straight lines needed to draw the given figure?
practice.solution: Each point of the star is made by two long lines, and each long line runs from one point to another. There are **5** such lines (the star can be drawn without lifting the pen, one line at a time).

practice.q: What is the minimum number of straight lines needed to draw the given figure?
practice.solution: The six-point star is two big triangles laid over each other. Each triangle has 3 sides, and each side runs straight through the star. Total = 3 + 3 = **6**.

practice.q: What is the minimum number of straight lines needed to draw the given figure?
practice.solution: The hexagon has 6 sides. The 3 long diagonals each join opposite corners and pass through the centre as one straight line each. Total = 6 + 3 = **9**.

practice.q: What is the minimum number of straight lines needed to draw the given figure?
practice.solution: There are 3 directions: horizontal, slanting left and slanting right. In each direction there is one line per row (3 rows → 3 lines). Total = 3 × 3 = **9**.

practice.q: What is the minimum number of straight lines needed to draw the given figure?
practice.solution: The pentagon has 5 sides and 5 diagonals (the star). Each is one straight line. Total = **10**.

practice.q: What is the minimum number of straight lines needed to draw the given figure?
practice.solution: The grid has 5 columns and 4 rows. Vertical lines = 5 + 1 = 6. Horizontal lines = 4 + 1 = 5. Total = **11**.

practice.q: What is the minimum number of straight lines needed to draw the given figure?
practice.solution: Grid: 5 vertical + 5 horizontal = 10. The two long diagonals run corner to corner: 2 more. Total = **12**.

practice.q: What is the minimum number of straight lines needed to draw the given figure?
practice.solution: Grid lines: 4 vertical + 4 horizontal = 8. Each cell has one diagonal going down to the right; diagonals that touch end to end lie on one straight path. The paths are: the main diagonal (3 pieces), two paths of 2 pieces and two of 1 piece = 5 lines. Total = 8 + 5 = **13**.
